events.text: One spring you come down out of the side channels and the river takes you: wide, cold, the colour of tea over black stones. There is a ford here where the ox carts cross at low water, a rope ferry for when the water is high, a ferry house with a smoking chimney, and below the ford a long pool with a bottom of black sand, like the bank you hatched from. The snake tastes the water for a long time and says nothing, which is how the snake says yes.

choices.text: Tortoise: settle in the black-sand pool below the ford, and stay

effects.log: You dig in until only the top of your shell shows, like one more black stone. The ferry goes over you twice a day. You decide you will be here when it stops.

choices.text: Snake: swim the whole stretch first, weir to weir, and count everything

effects.log: Three weirs, one mill race, eleven boats, the ferry, a drowned cart with an eel in it, and a heron that thinks it owns the ford. The snake comes back with the whole river by heart and lies down beside the tortoise in the black sand, satisfied.

choices.text: Both heads: lie at the lip of the ford, where you can watch the ferry and the pool at once

effects.log: The tortoise watches the pool. The snake watches the ferry. Between the two of you, nothing on this stretch of river will ever happen again without a witness.

events.text: The ferryman is a stooped old man the village calls Old Mun, who pulls the flat ferry across on a rope of twisted arrowroot vine and spits in the river every morning for luck. Once a month he pours a cup of rice liquor off the stern for the river god, and once a month the snake drinks it, and the river god, if there is one, says nothing about it.

choices.text: Tortoise: lie under the ferry in the spring current and hold it steady

effects.log: All spring the ferry crosses as if the river had gone tame. Old Mun tells the passengers his rope is the best on the river. It is a good rope. It is not that good.

choices.text: Snake: take the fish off his night line, one a week, never two

effects.log: Old Mun blames the otters, then the boys from the mill, then the river god. In the end he starts tying on a second hook, and the snake takes that fish too, out of principle.

choices.text: Let him see you once, sunning on the landing stone

effects.log: Old Mun sees a black shell the size of a winnowing tray and a black snake wound round it, both heads turned to look at him. He bows, very low, and from that day the cup of liquor comes every week.

events.text: In autumn the village drives bamboo stakes into the riverbed in a long V, the point downstream, and wattles the stakes with split bamboo. At the point of the V is a basket as big as a well-head, and every morning the men wade out and lift it, full of silver and thrashing. You fit through the gap at the point of the V. Only just.

choices.text: Snake: go in at night and eat from the basket like a lord

effects.log: The snake eats until it is a different shape. The men lift a basket of fish bones in the morning and stand looking at it for a long time. One of them says a word the snake has never heard before, and the snake keeps it.

choices.text: Tortoise: push one stake loose at the bottom, so half the river goes free

effects.log: One loose stake, and the weir leaks fish all season. The village catches enough, which is to say less than it wanted. The river below the ford is fuller than it has been in years.

choices.text: Leave the weir alone. It is their river too

effects.log: You lie upstream of the weir all autumn and watch them lift the basket. Children ride on their fathers' shoulders to see. You understand, a little, why a river is worth keeping.

events.text: Deep winter. The ford is frozen white and the carts cross on the ice to save the ferry fee. You lie under it in the dark, and hear every wheel go over. Then one does not go over: a salt carrier's ox steps on the thin place above the spring, and the ice goes, and the ox is in the water to its neck, bellowing, with the cart dragging it back by the yoke.

choices.text: Tortoise: get under the ox and push it up onto the shelf

ok.log: You put your shell under its belly and stand up in the black water. The ox comes out of the hole like a cork. The salt carrier never knows why, and gives half a sack of salt to the shrine in thanks, which the snake considers a waste.

fail.log: The ox kicks in its panic and catches your shell twice. The men on the ice get a rope round its horns in the end and drag it out. You go down to the bottom with a sore back and a lesson about oxen. (-10 health)

choices.text: Snake: bite through the cart's traces so the ox can swim free

effects.log: Two bites and the leather parts. The cart and the salt go to the bottom; the ox climbs out on its own. The salt carrier weeps for the salt. The ford tastes of it until spring.

choices.text: Watch. It is the river's business, and the ice's

effects.log: The men get it out with ropes, after a long time. You watch all of it from the bottom: the hole, the legs, the ropes, the steam off the ox. You find you remember every moment, as if it had been written somewhere.

events.text: There is an eddy under the cliff at the bend that turns all night, every night. One night the snake puts its head down into it and does not come up for a long time. When it does, it is shaking. It saw a small fishing boat with a patched brown sail, upside down in that eddy, and an old net tangled round the seat, and a funeral bell. Twelve springs from now, it says. Downriver, at the fishing village below the next ferry. It does not know how it knows. It only knows that it is true.

choices.text: Tortoise: "Then we go there, and we wait, and we see it"

effects.log: The tortoise turns its head downriver at once. Twelve years is nothing. The snake, who has never in its life been taken at its word, does not know what to do with its face. (The snake has read an omen: an ending under Emptiness, one journey downriver, in a few years. Go and Wait; be there when it comes, and write what you see.)

choices.text: Snake: look again, closer. Whose boat?

ok.log: Down again, into the cold. The sail has a patch of indigo cloth shaped like a fish. The man in the water has a laugh you can hear even drowning. (An omen under Emptiness: one journey downriver, in a few years. Go and Wait.)

fail.log: The eddy has the snake by the neck for a moment, and the tortoise has to drag both of you out. The snake saw nothing more, and swallowed half the river. (-4 health) (An omen under Emptiness: one journey downriver, in a few years. Go and Wait.)

choices.text: "A bad dream. Eddies are only water"

effects.log: The snake does not argue. It lies with its head on the shell and its eyes open all night. An omen does not need to be believed. (The omen stands: Emptiness, one journey downriver, in a few years.)

events.text: The snake goes downriver alone one night, as far as it can stretch from the shell and further, the way it has learned to do when the tortoise sleeps, and comes back before dawn cold to the bone. It found the village. It found the boat on the beach with the patched sail, and the fisherman mending it: a man of forty with a laugh like a dropped pot, and a daughter of seven who sits on the hull and hands him the cord.

choices.text: Tortoise: "Good. Now we know where to wait"

effects.log: The tortoise is already thinking about the mud below the landing, and how deep, and which side of the current. The snake wanted to talk about the daughter. It does not.

choices.text: Snake: tell the tortoise everything, the laugh, the daughter, the cord

effects.log: It takes until noon. The tortoise listens to all of it without a word, and at the end says: then we will see them both, when it comes. The snake had hoped it would say something else.

choices.text: Ask the snake why it is so cold

effects.log: It went too far from the shell, it says. That is all. You both know it is not all. Knowing where a man will die is a cold thing to carry home.

events.text: Years go by under the river, and the snake goes to look at the fishing village more often than it says. The daughter is taller than the mast now and goes out in the boat herself. The fisherman's laugh is the same. The eddy under the cliff is the same. "We could foul his nets the day before," the snake says one evening, to no one. "He would stay home and swear, and live."

choices.text: Tortoise: "We are going there to see, not to change"

effects.log: The snake says nothing for the rest of the season. It is the loudest nothing you have heard in years.

choices.text: Snake: "Then we will see. When the day comes"

effects.log: The tortoise does not answer, which is a kind of permission, and the snake knows it.

choices.text: Both heads: "We do not have to decide yet"

effects.log: You lie together in the black sand and agree on that one thing: not yet. It is a small agreement. It is warm, like a stone in the sun.

events.text: The day comes as the snake said it would: a grey morning, a north wind with sleet in it, and the river high and brown. The fisherman goes out alone because his daughter has a fever, laughing at the weather from the landing. You are where you have waited for years, in the mud below that landing. The boat with the patched sail goes out toward the cliff, and the eddy turns under it, slow as a millstone.

choices.text: Tortoise: watch. Every moment of it. That is what you came for

effects.log: The boat goes over. The net takes him. You see it all, and you do not look away, and that night something in the plate over your heart grows warm and then cold, and is written. (The Emptiness plate, written true: 1 of the 13 plates of your shell.)

choices.text: Snake: go into the eddy and shove the boat out of it

ok.log: The snake hauls, the tortoise has to follow or tear, and the boat skids out of the turning water onto the gravel. The fisherman sits in it, soaked, laughing like a dropped pot. No funeral, no plate. The tortoise says nothing all winter.

fail.log: The eddy is stronger than both of you. You are in it with him, close enough to see his face, and you cannot help. You see all of it. The plate over your heart is written that night. (-12 health) (The Emptiness plate, written true.)

choices.text: Both heads: the tortoise holds the keel while the snake pulls him out by the collar

effects.log: The boat goes down, empty. He comes up onto the gravel coughing river, with a black snake letting go of his collar and something huge going back under the water. No plate. Neither head minds, which surprises both of them.

events.text: The bier comes down to the river on the shoulders of eight men in hemp, with the bell-ringer walking ahead and singing the bier song, and the daughter walking first behind it in white. They bury him on the slope above the eddy so he can watch it. On your back, on the plate over your heart, the grain of the shell has changed. You can feel the shape of it in the water: a boat, a sail, a bell.

choices.text: Tortoise: read your own back, slowly, in the cold water

effects.log: It is all there, exactly as it was, not one thing added. You understand now what your shell is for. It is for this: to be the one place in the world where an ending is kept the way it happened.

choices.text: Snake: read it over, looking for something to improve

effects.log: The snake reads it three times and finds nothing to improve. This annoys it, and then it does not. "Twelve more," it says. "And the six for words." It has already counted.

choices.text: Go up and lie by the grave mound for a night

effects.log: In the morning the daughter finds a black turtle lying against her father's mound with frost on its shell. She does not chase it off. She brings it a bowl of rice and sits down beside it.

events.text: The bell rang downriver for three days and you were not there. You were one journey short. The snake heard it all from the river: the boat over in the eddy, white hemp on the water, the bier song. "I can write it," the snake says. "I know what it looked like. Near enough."

choices.text: Snake: let it write it, quick and neat

effects.log: The snake writes it from what the river says: quick, neat, and not quite true. The plate is written. The tortoise says nothing. It is the loudest nothing you have heard in years. (The Emptiness plate, cracked: it counts for every stage, but not for the Northern seat.)

choices.text: Tortoise: go now, late, and hear it from the mourners

ok.log: You arrive with the last of the mourners and lie in the shallows while they tell it over and over at the grave, the way people do. By the end you have it whole. You write it true. (-6 health) (The Emptiness plate, written true.)

fail.log: By the time you get there the mourners have gone home and the grave is a mound of new turf. Nobody tells a turtle anything. You leave the plate bare. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let it go. It was not yours to write

effects.log: The plate stays bare. The snake thinks this is a waste of a perfectly good ending. The tortoise thinks a plate is not a thing you fill. They are both a little right.

events.text: The fisherman comes up the river in his boat one spring, years later, with grey in his hair and the same laugh, and ties up at the cliff above the eddy, and pours a whole jar of rice liquor into it. "I do not know what you are," he says to the water. "My daughter says a black turtle. I say a river god. Either way." He bows to the eddy, which is the wrong place, and goes home.

choices.text: Snake: drink the jar, every drop

effects.log: The snake is happy for a week and useless for two. "There is still an ending in him somewhere," it says, hiccupping. "There always is. We only moved it." The tortoise agrees, and is glad anyway.

choices.text: Tortoise: come up beside the boat, once, so he knows

effects.log: He sees the shell come up beside him, black and wet, with the snake round it. He stops laughing for the first time in his life. Then he laughs harder than ever, and tells it in every tavern on the river until he dies, at eighty, in his bed.

events.text: The first hard frost comes down on the river, and something on your back aches. Not the shell, which never aches. A plate. The one the snake wrote without seeing. In the cold you can feel the crack through it, thin as a hair, running right through the middle of the words, and the words on each side of it do not quite meet.

choices.text: Snake: "It is a small crack. It counts"

effects.log: It does count. The snake is right. The tortoise lies in the frost and feels the crack all night, the way a tongue keeps going back to a broken tooth.

choices.text: Tortoise: say nothing, and feel it

effects.log: You lie still and let it ache. The snake waits for the tortoise to say something. The tortoise does not. By morning the snake is sorrier than any words could have made it.

choices.text: Both heads: "We will go back for it. Not now. But we will"

effects.log: The snake agrees before the tortoise has finished. It is not a promise to mend it tomorrow. It is a promise that the crack will not be the last word.

events.text: The snake explains, in the end, because the tortoise will not ask. It wrote the plate to save you a journey: a long one, a cold one, upstream in a flood year, with catchers on the banks. It was being kind. It was being quick. With the snake those have always been the same thing.

choices.text: Tortoise: "I know. I forgive it. The plate does not"

effects.log: The snake winds one turn tighter round the shell that night. It is the nearest thing to an apology a snake has.

choices.text: Tortoise: "Never again. Not one more plate you did not see"

effects.log: The snake hisses that it will write what it likes on a back it also lives on. The tortoise draws its head in and does not come out for three days. The Knot is looser by spring.

choices.text: Snake: "And I would do it again. You are slow, and the endings are not"

effects.log: It is true, and that is the worst of it. The tortoise turns the words over all winter and cannot find the crack in them.

events.text: A village schoolteacher crossing the ford in low water sees the characters on your back, sunning on the landing stone, and stops dead with one shoe off. He crouches and reads them aloud to the children behind him, slowly, the way he teaches. He reads the cracked plate last. He frowns. "That is not how it happened," he says. "I was there."

choices.text: Tortoise: stay, and let him read it all

effects.log: He tells the children how it really happened, standing in the ford with his shoe in his hand. You listen to every word of it. Now you know what the true plate should say. You only have to go and be sure.

choices.text: Snake: slide off the stone into the river before he finishes

effects.log: The children shriek; the teacher drops his shoe in the river. Nobody finishes reading anything. The tortoise is furious all the way to the bottom.

events.text: There is only one way to mend a plate the snake wrote without seeing: go back to the place of the ending, the long way, and find the people who remember it, and write over the lie with what they say. It costs a season, and the cold, and your strength. The tortoise has been ready for years. The snake has been ready since the schoolteacher.

choices.text: Tortoise: go back the long way, now

ok.log: A season upriver in the frost, and an old woman on a ferry landing who saw it all and has been waiting for somebody to ask. You write the truth over the lie. The crack closes like ice closing over a hole. (-12 health) (Your first cracked plate is mended.)

fail.log: You go back. The ones who remember are dead or gone to the city. The crack aches all the way home. Next winter, the tortoise says. Write on the Shell will take you back again. (-12 health)

choices.text: Snake: "It counts. Leave it, and climb"

effects.log: You leave it. You climb. The crack aches every frost, and every frost the tortoise says nothing about it, and the snake hears every word.

events.text: One autumn dusk something goes through the river that is not a sound. Every fish in the pool turns its head the same way. The eels come out from under the stones. The old carp of the deep hole rises, which it has not done in your lifetime. Upstream, the river's own lord is calling, the old water god of the north, and he is calling everything that has a back.
events.arc: The Bridge of Fish and Turtles

choices.text: Tortoise: go where the others go

effects.log: Upstream, with half the river: carp and catfish and mandarin fish and a hundred soft-shelled turtles you did not know lived here. Nobody explains. Everybody hurries. You go slowly, and arrive anyway.

choices.text: Snake: find out why first

effects.log: The snake asks an eel, who asks a carp, who says: the river lord's grandchild is in trouble at the crossing, and the river lord is old and proud and wants his grandchild across. The snake is interested at once. It loves a family quarrel.

choices.text: Stay in your pool. The river lord is not your lord

effects.log: The pool empties of everything but you and the heron. In the morning the fish come back tired and talking all at once, and you have missed whatever it was.

events.text: The crossing is wide and fast and there is no bridge. Four riders come down to the bank at a gallop, and behind them on the plain a long line of dust: horsemen, many, with spears. The first rider is young, with a bow taller than he is. He rides into the shallows, strikes the water with the bow, and shouts at it: he is the son of heaven and the grandson of this river, and the river will not let him die here. All round you, every fish and every turtle in the river rises.
events.arc: The Bridge of Fish and Turtles

choices.text: Rise with them

effects.log: You come up into the air between a carp and a turtle half your size, and your shell locks against theirs, and theirs against the next, all the way across. You are a bridge. You have never been part of anything before.

choices.text: Snake: rise, but at the far end, where the pursuers will step first

effects.log: The snake chooses the place with care: the last stone of the bridge, the first one an enemy foot will find. The tortoise does not ask why. It does not need to.

choices.text: Stay under. One turtle in a thousand will not be missed

effects.log: You lie on the bottom and watch the underside of a bridge of bellies go over. Four horses cross on it. Then the bridge comes down in a rain of fish, and the snake will not speak to you until the ice.

events.text: The first horse steps onto the bridge of backs. You feel it come, shell by shell, a weight going over the river like a slow wave, and then it is on you: four iron-shod hooves and a rider and a bow, the whole weight of a kingdom that does not exist yet, standing on your back.
events.arc: The Bridge of Fish and Turtles

choices.text: Tortoise: hold. Do not even breathe

ok.log: You hold. The hooves go over, one, two, three, four, and on to the next back. The rider never looks down. You have never been so heavy, or so proud of it.

fail.log: A hoof comes down on the edge of your shell and something in your shoulder gives. You hold anyway. The horse goes on. You bleed into the river for a week. (-15 health)

choices.text: Snake: lie flat along the shell and keep the horse calm, eye to eye

effects.log: The horse looks down and sees a black snake looking up at it, very calm, very close. It decides, the way horses do, that everything is fine, and walks on without a stumble.

choices.text: Both heads: hold together, the tortoise the weight and the snake the balance

effects.log: The tortoise takes the weight; the snake shifts it, left and right, so it never lands in one place. The horse crosses you like a bridge of stone.

events.text: The four are across, on the far bank, turning their horses. The pursuers reach the near bank and their captain rides straight onto the bridge, and the river, all at once, lets go: every fish and every turtle sinks. The bridge is gone. The captain's horse is up to its chest in a river that was a road a moment ago. On the far bank the young archer laughs.
events.arc: The Bridge of Fish and Turtles

choices.text: Sink with the others, and watch the crossing end from below

effects.log: You go down with the bridge and look up through the brown water at the hooves of the pursuers thrashing where the road was. A crossing made and unmade in one morning. That night the plate over your left shoulder is written. (The Ox plate: a crossing, written true.)

choices.text: Snake: stay up one moment more, under the captain's horse, then dive

effects.log: The horse finds one stone of the bridge still there, and puts its weight on it, and the stone goes away. The captain goes into the river in his armour. His men pull him out by the hair. You saw all of it, from very close. (The Ox plate: a crossing, written true.)

choices.text: Both heads: hold up the last straggler first, a companion with a lame horse, then sink

effects.log: One rider was still on the bridge, the slowest, with a lame horse. You stay up under him alone with spears coming. He makes the bank. You sink with an arrow in the edge of your shell. (-6 health) (The Ox plate: a crossing, written true.)

events.text: Ten years on, barges come down the river with new banners, and the fish say a town has been built on the far side of the crossing, with walls of rammed earth and a hall on a hill. The young archer is a king there. He has a kingdom with a name. The fish argue about whose back he crossed on. Every carp in the river claims it was theirs.
events.arc: The Bridge of Fish and Turtles

choices.text: Tortoise: say nothing. You know whose back it was

effects.log: One of a thousand. It is enough to know it. The tortoise does not need the carp to know.

choices.text: Snake: claim it loudly, with the hoof-mark as proof

effects.log: There is a mark on the shell, a crescent, exactly a hoof's width. The carp go very quiet. The snake shows it to everyone who passes for a year, and to some of them twice.

events.text: At the crossing where the bridge rose, the people of the new kingdom have set up a stone carved with fish and turtles, and every spring they come down to the bank and throw live fish back into the river and never eat turtle. An old woman tells the story to her grandchildren on the bank: one thousand backs, she says, and not one of them asked for anything. You are lying in the shallows under her feet.
events.arc: The Bridge of Fish and Turtles

choices.text: Lie still and listen to your own story

effects.log: In her telling the turtles are all the same size and the river lord appears in person, in a hat. It is wrong in every detail and right in the only one that matters.

choices.text: Show the grandchildren the hoof-mark on your shell

effects.log: The children see a black turtle come up out of the river and turn so the sun shows a crescent pressed into its shell. The old woman stops in the middle of a word and bows to the river. The children never forget it, and neither, it turns out, do their children.

events.text: {npc} comes to the ford with six men, a cart, and a cage of split bamboo. A diviner of the royal observatory, by the seal on {his} belt and the soot under {his} nails. The court's brazier has cracked its last good shell, and the readings from young shells are thin and quarrelsome. The court wants a hundred-year shell. {He} pays the ferry family a string of coins to say where the old turtle of the ford lies, and they say, after a long look at each other, that there is no such turtle.

choices.text: Tortoise: draw in and lie like a stone in the black sand

effects.log: {npc} walks the bank for three days, prodding the shallows with a pole. Twice the pole knocks on your shell. Twice {he} moves on. {He} is patient. So are you. You are better at it.

choices.text: Snake: watch {him} from the reeds, all of it

effects.log: {npc} eats alone, sleeps little, and in the evenings heats a small shell over a charcoal pot and reads the cracks, frowning. The snake learns more about divination in a week than the fortune-teller at the market taught it in a year.

choices.text: Leave the ford for a season

effects.log: A cold season in a side channel full of leeches. When you come back, the ferry family have a new roof and are very careful not to look at the pool.

events.text: {npc} has stopped asking and started building. A fence of cut reeds from the bank out into the river, slanting, so anything walking along the bottom is led, gently, into a funnel of net. At the end of the funnel, a basket of river snails. The snails are very fresh. The tortoise has not eaten in a week.

choices.text: Tortoise: go round the end of the fence, the long way, in deep water

ok.log: The long way round, half a day in water so cold your eyes ache. You come out upstream of the fence with nobody the wiser. {npc} lifts an empty net in the morning and, to your surprise, laughs.

fail.log: The deep water has a second fence in it that you did not see. The net closes over you like a fist. Men shout. You are lifted into the air, streaming, into the lamplight.

choices.text: Snake: go into the funnel first and bite through the end of the net

ok.log: The snake chews the net open at the knot and you walk out through the snails, eating as you go. In the morning {npc} holds up the bitten net and looks at the river for a long time.

fail.log: The net is doubled. The snake bites through one layer and not the second, and the men are already wading out with lanterns.

choices.text: Snake: take the bait. You want to see the brazier

effects.log: The snake walks you into the funnel on purpose, over the tortoise's furious silence. The net closes. The snake is very calm. The tortoise will remember this for two hundred years.

events.text: A reed hut on the bank, a bronze brazier, and you on your back on a board with your plates to the fire. {npc} heats a bronze rod until it glows and holds it to your belly-plate, waiting for the crack that will tell the court whether the coming year is good. The shell is a hundred years thick. It is taking its time.

choices.text: Tortoise: endure. A hundred-year shell does not crack for one rod

effects.log: The rod glows, cools, glows. The shell will not crack. By dawn {npc} is sitting back on {his} heels, staring. {He} has never seen a shell that would not answer. Then {he} says, quietly, "Perhaps that is the answer." (-15 health)

choices.text: Snake: write in the ash with your body

mem.note: wrote my future in the ash

ok.log: The snake slides off the board into the spilled ash and lies in the shape of a character, then another: the year of {npc}'s own death, and the name of the person who will be with {him}. {npc} reads it, sits down, and does not pick up the rod again.

fail.log: The snake tries to write and the men think it is trying to bite, and pin it with a forked stick. It writes nothing. The rod comes down again. (-10 health)

choices.text: Both heads: the tortoise braces against the board while the snake hooks the brazier over

effects.log: The brazier goes over, the coals hit the wet floor, and the hut fills with steam and shouting. You are off the board, out of the door and into the river before anyone can see through the white. (-6 health)

events.text: Morning, and the reed hut is quiet. {npc} comes out, unties you from the board, carries you down to the water {him}self, which is not easy, and sets you in the shallows. Then {he} sits on the bank with {his} knees up and watches you not leave.

choices.text: Tortoise: stay a moment, and look at {him}

mem.note: stayed in the shallows and looked at me

effects.log: You look at each other for a long time, an old shell and a tired diviner. Then {npc} nods, as if a reading had come out, and goes back up the bank and breaks the cage.

choices.text: Snake: hiss once, so {he} remembers

effects.log: {npc} flinches, then laughs, the way people laugh when they are let off something. {He} goes back to court and tells them the old turtle of the ford is a myth.

events.text: Twenty years on, {npc} comes back to the ford alone, white-haired, without men or cage or cart, and sits on the landing stone. {He} has left the observatory. {He} has brought a bundle of old cracked plastrons, every reading {he} ever made, and one by one {he} drops them into your pool. "Every one of them came true," {he} says to the water. "I would like them to stop."

choices.text: Tortoise: come up and lie beside the stone while {he} does it

effects.log: One shell after another goes into the black sand. You lie beside the stone until the bundle is empty. {npc} puts a hand on your back, once, very lightly, the way you would touch a shell you were not going to heat.

choices.text: Snake: read the cracks as they sink

effects.log: Wars, harvests, a queen's fever, a bridge that fell. All true, all over. The snake reads them like old letters. {npc} watches it reading and understands, finally, what has been lying in the black sand all this time.

choices.text: Draw in. Some people are best left alone with their regrets

effects.log: {npc} drops the last shell, sits until dusk, and walks away up the road without looking back. The plastrons lie in your pool for a hundred years. You sleep on them.

events.text: The river you followed south runs under the walls of a royal city, and you slept the winter in the bank of its palace pond. You wake in lantern light with earth falling off your shell. A ghost ran through the palace crying that the kingdom will fall, the gardeners are whispering, and sank into the ground, and the king had them dig where it sank, and three feet down they found you. On your back, in ink that will not wash off, someone has written: the kingdom is a full moon; its rival is a new moon. The snake swears on the egg it did not write it.

choices.text: Tortoise: look at the snake for a very long time

effects.log: The snake looks back, wide-eyed, offended, and then frightened, because it really did not write it, and if it did not, who did?

choices.text: Snake: read it again, and think what it means

effects.log: A full moon. A new moon. The snake turns it over all night in the bronze basin they put you in. A full moon is as big as it will ever be. The snake does not like where that goes.

choices.text: Both heads: "It does not matter who wrote it. It is true"

effects.log: You both feel it, under the ink: an ending, close, in this city. Not an omen the snake read. One that came and found you.

events.text: The king sits on a high seat in a hall of red pillars and has the basin carried in, and you in it, and calls for the court shaman to read your back. The shaman is old and does not hurry. "A full moon is full," the shaman says. "Full things wane. A new moon is new. New things wax." The hall goes silent. The king says one word, and the guards take the shaman out by the arms, and the shaman does not come back.

choices.text: Tortoise: watch the shaman's face as they take them out

effects.log: There is no fear in it. Only the look of someone who has said the true thing in the wrong room and knew it was the wrong room before they started. You remember that face for a thousand years.

choices.text: Snake: hiss at the king, loud enough for the hall

effects.log: Every courtier hears a turtle hiss at the king. Nobody says so. The king has the basin covered with a cloth, which is what kings do with things they would rather not hear.

choices.text: Draw both heads in. This is not a room for a turtle to be noticed in

effects.log: Shut in your shell in a bronze basin, you hear the rest through the metal: a long silence, then a new voice, smooth as oil, asking for permission to speak.

events.text: The new voice belongs to a courtier with a soft beard. A full moon, the courtier explains, is strength. A new moon is weakness. Plainly, the kingdom is at its height and the rival is a sliver. The king is delighted, and gives the courtier a silk robe, and has you put in the palace pond as a lucky turtle, with a gold ribbon on your shell. The snake laughs. It is a sound like a kettle, and only the tortoise hears it.

choices.text: Tortoise: stay in the palace pond. Someone should see how this ends

effects.log: You settle into the palace pond under the lotus, with your ridiculous gold ribbon, and wait. The tortoise is good at waiting. It is the snake who counts the days.

choices.text: Snake: slip out by the drain to the river, tonight

effects.log: There is a drain under the pond wall with an iron grille the snake can just get through, and you can just not. It takes until dawn and a bent grille. By sunrise you are in the river, the ribbon floating behind you.

choices.text: Both heads: stay, but the snake keeps watch on the walls

effects.log: The tortoise lies in the pond; the snake lies along the coping with its head on the wall and its eyes on the plain. It sees the dust long before the watchmen do.

events.text: That summer the armies come, two of them, from the sea and from the east. The palace burns on the last night, the red pillars first, then the roofs, the great roof of the hall falling in all at once with a sound like a breath let out. Treasury carts on the road, court ladies running, a gold ribbon on a turtle in a pond full of floating ash. The full moon is waning, all at once, in one night.

choices.text: Tortoise: stay in the pond, under the lotus, and watch it all

effects.log: You watch every roof go. You do not look away once. By morning the pond is grey with ash and the plate across the top of your shell is written, every beam of it. (The Rooftop plate: a house falling, written true.)

choices.text: Snake: now, out through the drain, before the walls fall

effects.log: The snake drags you out under the burning wall. The tortoise fights it the whole way, and loses. From the river you see the glow over the city all night. You did not stay.

choices.text: Both heads: carry a little page who fell in the pond to the bank, then come back and watch

effects.log: A child in court silk, face down among the lotus. The snake gets the collar, the tortoise swims for the steps. The child runs into the smoke, alive. You come back and watch the rest. (-8 health) (The Rooftop plate, written true.)

events.text: From the river you see the glow over the royal city all night, and smoke all the next day, and on the third day the barges come down with soldiers in strange armour, singing. You were not there when the roofs fell. "I can write it," the snake says. "I know what fire looks like."

choices.text: Snake: let it write the Rooftop plate from the glow

effects.log: The snake writes a palace falling from smoke and a glow and soldiers singing on barges. It is a good plate. It is not true. It cracks in the first frost. (The Rooftop plate, cracked.)

choices.text: Tortoise: go back into the ash, and see what is left

ok.log: Through the burned water gate at night, into a pond grey with ash. An old gardener is sitting by it, the one who dug you up, and tells the whole night to the pond because there is no one else. You listen until the end. (-8 health) (The Rooftop plate, written true.)

fail.log: Soldiers on the walls with bows, and you a black shell on grey ash. An arrow skids off your back. You go back to the river with nothing written. (-12 health)

choices.text: Let it go. The city is not yours to write

effects.log: You turn north and swim home. Somewhere behind you a kingdom is finished, and you do not carry it. The tortoise wonders, for a long time, whether that is wisdom or only a turtle being slow.

events.text: A summer of a strange pull, south: the river runs to the sea, the sea runs south along a warm coast, and one night you crawl up out of a southern river onto a small hill above a valley of nine villages. In the morning you see what you are lying on. The hill is exactly the shape of a turtle's head, with its neck stretched out from the mountain behind it. The valley calls it Turtle Peak, and you are on the crown.
events.arc: Turtle, Turtle, Put Forth Your Head

choices.text: Tortoise: dig in on the crown, and stay till spring

effects.log: The earth on the crown is soft and warm and smells of pine. You sleep the winter in it like a seed. The snake keeps one eye open, because the hill feels as if it is waiting for something.

choices.text: Snake: find out why a hill is shaped like that

effects.log: The villagers say it was named long before anyone counted chiefs. The nine villages have nine chiefs and no king, and every spring the chiefs climb it to purify themselves in the stream below. The snake thinks that is a lot of chiefs for one valley.

events.text: The day of the spring purification. Nine chiefs and two hundred people climb Turtle Peak, and a voice from the sky that is not yours tells them to dig the top of the hill and sing. They dig, with their hands, all round you. Then they sing, stamping: "Turtle, turtle, put forth your head! If you do not put it forth, we will roast you and eat you!" Two hundred people, looking straight down at you. Both of you have a head.
events.arc: Turtle, Turtle, Put Forth Your Head

choices.text: Tortoise: put forth the tortoise head, slowly, with dignity

effects.log: An old turtle's head comes out of the earth, blinking, wrinkled, entirely calm. The singing stops. The oldest chief begins to weep. The snake, still inside, is livid.

choices.text: Snake: put forth the snake head, fast

effects.log: A black snake's head comes out of the pit with its tongue flickering. Two hundred people take one step back. The tortoise, still inside, is mortified.

choices.text: Both heads: put forth both, together, facing each other

effects.log: Two heads come out of the earth at once and turn to look at each other, as if to check, and then turn together to look at the crowd. Nobody in the valley will ever agree on what they saw. Everybody agrees it counted.

choices.text: Draw both in, and wait to see what they do

effects.log: They sing it again, louder. And again. Somebody fetches dry pine for a fire, half as a joke. Then the sky goes bright overhead, and nobody is looking at you any more.

events.text: Nine chiefs stand round the pit arguing, as chiefs do, about what just happened. The oldest says the song said turtle and a turtle answered. The youngest says the song said head, and whose head, and does a snake count. A third says that if it does not count they will have to roast something, and nobody brought salt.
events.arc: Turtle, Turtle, Put Forth Your Head

choices.text: Snake: hiss the last line of the song back at them

effects.log: "...we will roast you and eat you," says a snake from a hole, in no language at all, and every one of the nine understands it perfectly. The argument is over.

choices.text: Tortoise: lie still until they decide

effects.log: It takes most of the morning. They decide it counted, and that the youngest chief should apologise to the hill, which the youngest chief does, very formally.

choices.text: Put forth both heads, to settle it

effects.log: Now there are two heads out of the pit, and the youngest chief sits down on the grass and says nothing for the rest of the day.

events.text: Out of the bright sky comes a cord, purple, thin as a bowstring, lowering something wrapped in red cloth. It comes down slowly, swinging a little, and settles on the earth in front of the pit, in front of you. The red cloth falls open. A golden box. Two hundred people lie face down in the grass. You are the only one left looking at it.
events.arc: Turtle, Turtle, Put Forth Your Head

choices.text: Tortoise: guard it, and let no hand touch it till the chiefs come

effects.log: You lie across the cord with the box against your shell. When the chiefs at last get up and come forward on their knees, you move aside. The oldest chief bows to you before he bows to the box.

choices.text: Snake: taste the cord

effects.log: It tastes of the sky, if the sky were silk: cold and high and a little like rain. The snake never tells anyone. It does not have words for it yet, and when it has, it chooses not to.

choices.text: Both heads: look at the box together, and listen to it

effects.log: There is something in it. Six somethings, each with a heartbeat, each quicker than yours. One egg, two hearts, you think, and something in both of you goes tender.

events.text: The box goes down to the chiefs' houses wrapped in its red cloth, and in twelve days the six golden eggs in it hatch into six boys, who grow as if the days were years. The first to come out is tall by summer, and the nine chiefs make him king of the valley and call him Suro, and the other five go off to be kings of their own valleys. Every spring after, the people climb Turtle Peak and sing the song. They sing it to the hill. You know better.
events.arc: Turtle, Turtle, Put Forth Your Head

choices.text: Sleep on the crown every spring, and hear the song

effects.log: Every spring two hundred voices sing at you to put forth your head, and every spring you do, a little, and the children shriek. It becomes the best day of your year.

choices.text: Go home to the north. A king does not need a turtle

effects.log: You crawl down the hill and back into the river and north for a year. Behind you a valley has a king, and a hill has a story, and you have a feeling, that will not go, that you will be sung for again.

events.text: The young king pulls down the nine villages' palisades, one by one, to raise one wall round one town at the foot of Turtle Peak. The nine chiefs are old men now, and stand by their gates as the stakes come out of the ground, and watch the age of nine chiefs end. It is not sad, exactly. It is not anything else, either.
events.arc: Turtle, Turtle, Put Forth Your Head

choices.text: Watch the last palisade come down

effects.log: The last stake comes out of the last village. The oldest chief carries it to the new wall himself and sets it in the rammed earth. You see it go in. The plate low on your shell is written. (The Encampment plate: a capital's works and an old order ending, written true.)

choices.text: Snake: go before it ends, and write it later from the songs

effects.log: The snake writes it from the songs: grander, sadder, with a speech the old chief never made. It cracks in the first frost. (The Encampment plate, cracked.)

choices.text: Leave it. It is the valley's ending, not yours

effects.log: You go north before the wall is finished. The snake says that was a whole plate thrown in the river. The tortoise says some endings belong to the people who live through them.

events.text: {npc} is a wandering swordsman who sold the sword and kept the scabbard, and makes a living in market towns with a fan and a small drum, telling stories: the tiger who smoked a pipe, the filial daughter, the rabbit and the turtle. {He} cannot afford the inn, so {he} sleeps under the plank bridge over your ford, every night, for a year, and practises the stories out loud to the river.

choices.text: Snake: listen, every night, to every word

effects.log: The snake lies along the bridge pile with its head an arm's length from {npc}'s ear and does not miss a syllable. By the third month it knows which stories {he} tells badly. By the sixth it knows why.

choices.text: Tortoise: sleep through it, and let the stories go over you like water

effects.log: The tortoise sleeps. The stories go into it anyway, the way the river does, and years later it will find it knows the tiger who smoked a pipe by heart, and not know how.

choices.text: Push driftwood up the bank to {his} fire

effects.log: Every night there is a little more wood by the fire than {npc} gathered. {He} thanks the river god in the middle of a story, and goes back to the story without missing a beat.

events.text: The tortoise wakes one night to a strange feeling in the snake's throat, which is also, a little, its own: the snake is moving its mouth along with {npc}. Not hissing. Shaping. The tiger said to the woodcutter. The tiger said. The tiger. The snake does not know the tortoise is awake.

choices.text: Tortoise: pretend to sleep, and let it practise

effects.log: You lie still for a whole winter of nights while the snake learns to shape words with a mouth that was never made for them. You do not say anything. It would be like waking someone in the middle of a prayer.

choices.text: Tortoise: "What are you doing?"

effects.log: The snake jerks as if bitten and does not move its mouth again for a month. Then, because it cannot help it, it starts again, more quietly, when it thinks you really are asleep.

choices.text: Snake: practise louder. Let the tortoise hear

effects.log: "The ti-ger," says the snake, out loud, into the dark under the bridge. {npc} stops snoring. Then starts again. The snake is pleased with itself for a week.

events.text: One night under the bridge {npc} stops in the middle of the tiger who smoked a pipe, because {he} cannot remember what the tiger said next. {He} says, "The tiger said, the tiger said..." into the dark, and taps the drum, and cannot find it. And the river says it.

choices.text: Snake: say the tiger's line, exactly

effects.log: {npc} sits bolt upright. Then, because {he} is a professional, {he} says the line back, and finishes the story, all of it, to the end, and only then puts down the drum and says, very carefully: "Thank you."

choices.text: Snake: say "Thank you" first, for a year of stories

effects.log: The first word a black snake ever says to a human is thanks. {npc} weeps, which surprises both of you, and then tells the river every story {he} knows all over again, properly, as a gift.

choices.text: Snake: say {his} name, which it learned from {his} muttering

effects.log: A name out of the dark under a bridge. {npc} grabs the scabbard {he} no longer has a sword for. Then {he} laughs, shakily, and asks the river how long it has been listening. "A year," says the snake. "You tell the rabbit badly."

events.text: The tortoise does not sleep for a month. A voice is a door, and the snake has opened it, and now anything can come through: questions, bargains, humans with words for you to carry, humans who will know there is someone in the river to ask. The tortoise has no voice of its own. Everything it ever says to a human from now on, the snake will have to say for it.

choices.text: Tortoise: "Then say it for me, and say it true"

effects.log: The snake promises. It is the first promise between you with words in it. It is heavier than you expected, and lighter than you feared.

choices.text: Tortoise: draw in, and do not come out till the snake is quiet

effects.log: You stay in the shell for the whole spring. The snake talks to {npc} every night, over your head, about stories, and the tortoise inside hears every word and is not part of any of them.

choices.text: Snake: "I will speak. You will decide what I say"

effects.log: It is a fair offer. It is also the snake, who will decide a great deal on the way from the tortoise to the human. You both know that. You take the offer anyway.

events.text: {npc} has pulled the ferry at your ford for fifty years, like {his} father and {his} father's father before {him}, back to the old man who first spat in the river for luck. Now {he} lies on a straw mat on the bank where {he} can hear the rope creak, and asks the river to listen, because the village says the river answers now. Thirty years ago {his} only child cursed {him} on this landing over an ox, and went north to the war, and never wrote. "Tell them," {npc} says. "If they come back. Tell them I was wrong about the ox. Tell them I forgave the rest before they reached the far bank."

choices.text: Snake: "Give me the word. I will keep it until they come"

mem.note: took my word for my child

effects.log: The snake says it back to {him}, every word, so {he} knows it is held. {npc} closes {his} eyes. "The ox was lame," {he} says. "They were right. Tell them that too." The snake adds it. (A word to keep: wait for the child, and carry it.)

choices.text: Tortoise, through the snake: "We will be here. We are always here"

effects.log: The snake says it in the tortoise's way, slowly, which is not the snake's way at all, and {npc} hears the difference and smiles. "Two of you," {he} says. "Good. One to remember and one to remind." (A word to keep: wait for the child, and carry it.)

choices.text: "We have no road north. Give it to someone with legs"

effects.log: {npc} nods as if {he} expected it, and asks the river to listen anyway, and tells it the whole story of the ox, and dies before the ice. The snake is quiet all winter. The tortoise was right, and it does not feel right.

events.text: The old ferryman is buried on the slope above the landing, facing the rope, and for a season there is nobody to pull the ferry. People shout across from the far bank and nobody comes. The rope sags into the current. On the near bank, a market woman with a basket of eggs sits on the landing stone and cries, because it is market day.

choices.text: Tortoise: take the rope in your mouth and pull the ferry yourself, all season

effects.log: The ferry crosses empty-handed, with nobody at the rope, all season. People get on, very carefully, and get off on the far bank, and do not discuss it. The market woman's eggs arrive unbroken.

choices.text: Snake: tell the village headman, from the well, to find a new ferryman

effects.log: The headman hears a voice in the well telling him to get on with it. He gets on with it. A nephew from upriver takes the rope by spring, and is told, by everyone, to spit in the river for luck.

choices.text: Lie under the landing and keep the word warm

effects.log: "I was wrong about the ox. The ox was lame. They were right." The snake says it over to the tortoise every night under the landing, so neither of you lets go of a single word of it.

events.text: The word is heavy in a way nothing on your back has been. A plate is an ending. A word is a door held open for someone who has not come yet. North, the snake says, in the war: an army that does not come home because it has nowhere to come home to. So you go north, a journey at a time, past garrison towns where soldiers wash their feet in the river and talk about the ferries they grew up beside.

choices.text: Tortoise: listen at every garrison ford for a ferry voice

effects.log: At a ford three journeys north, an old soldier washing a pot says the word "ox" in the accent of your river, and laughs at something, and you lose them in the crowd. The snake says: closer.

choices.text: Snake: ask the soldiers from under the bank, at night

ok.log: A frightened sentry tells the river everything it asks: which unit, which camp, which old soldier from which ferry town keeps a ferry rope knot tied on a string round their neck. The snake knows who you are carrying the word to now.

fail.log: The sentry runs for the captain, and the captain sends men with spears and torches to find the talking river. You go downstream fast and quiet. Soldiers are worse than diviners. Diviners want you whole.

events.text: They come down to the landing in the evening: an old soldier with a stiff leg and a grey topknot and a ferry-rope knot on a string round the neck, who stands looking at the ferry and the grave on the slope for a long time. The snake lifts its head out of the water. The soldier does not run. Perhaps soldiers stop running from things, after long enough.

choices.text: Snake: say the word exactly as it was given, the ox and all

effects.log: "I was wrong about the ox. The ox was lame. You were right. I forgave the rest before you reached the far bank." The soldier sits down on the landing stone in the dark and does not get up for a long time. (The first word kept, written true on your back: a word plate.)

choices.text: Snake: say something kinder. "The old ferryman was proud of you, every day"

effects.log: The soldier weeps with gratitude. It is a kind thing, and it is not what was said, and the ox is not in it. The tortoise hears every word it is not. The plate cracks in the first frost. (A word plate, cracked.)

choices.text: Both heads: the exact word, and then the tortoise's own: "We waited thirty years to give it to you"

effects.log: The snake says the old ferryman's words, and then the tortoise's, slower, in a voice the snake has to search for. The soldier puts a hand on the black shell and says thank you to both of you, separately. (The first word kept, written true.)

events.text: The old soldier does not go back north. In spring there is a new ferryman at your ford with a stiff leg and a grey topknot, who pulls the rope badly, swears at it, and every morning spits in the river for luck and then says, to the water, "Morning, both of you."

choices.text: Tortoise: hold the ferry steady under that bad pulling, every flood

effects.log: The worst ferryman on the river has the steadiest ferry. Nobody can explain it. The soldier can, and does not.

choices.text: Snake: answer "Morning" back, every morning

effects.log: For years the ferry crossing at your ford begins with a greeting and an answer. Passengers think the ferryman is talking to himself. The ferryman lets them.

events.text: Too late. A soldier you do not know comes down to the landing with a bundle: a ferry-rope knot on a string, a spoon, a name written on a strip of board. The one the word was for died in the north the winter before last, of a fever, in a garrison by a frozen river. This soldier promised to bring the things home to the ferry. There is nobody at the ferry to give them to.

choices.text: Tortoise: take the bundle down to the grave on the slope, and say the word there

effects.log: You lay the spoon and the knot on the old ferryman's mound, and the snake says the word to the turf: I was wrong about the ox. It is not written on your back. It is said, which is a different thing, and perhaps enough.

choices.text: Snake: tell the soldier the word instead, so somebody living hears it

effects.log: The soldier listens to a black snake tell a story about an ox and a father, and at the end says, "They talked about that ox every night for years." So they had been forgiving each other the whole time, at either end of the war.

events.text: {npc}, a cloth merchant with a boat full of silk, is held on the near bank by the magistrate's order: no crossings while the levy is gathered. On the far bank, in the village with the big willow, there is a bride waiting who was promised to {him} before the levy, and the wedding was to be this month. {npc} has heard about the turtle at the ford. {He} ties a letter to your shell with a red cord, folded small and oiled against the water.

choices.text: Tortoise: carry it across, slow and dry

effects.log: You swim the river with your head up and the letter riding high. {npc} watches from the bank until you are a black dot, and then until you are not.

choices.text: Snake: carry it, and read it on the way

effects.log: Halfway across, the snake works the fold open with its nose. It can read: it taught itself on the notices nailed to the ferry-house door. The tortoise is appalled. The snake keeps reading.

choices.text: "Not across a levy line. Find a boat"

effects.log: {npc} unties the letter and sits on the bank with it in {his} lap. You feel, absurdly, that you have refused something important, and that it will come back.

events.text: Midriver, the letter on your back. The snake has read it, or is reading it now, out loud to the tortoise. It is terrible. A list of the silks {npc} has in the boat, with prices. A complaint about the magistrate. A long passage about {his} mother's knees. And at the end, one line, plain: I counted the days to the wedding on the stern post with a knife, and I will keep counting.

choices.text: Tortoise: deliver it as written. All of it, the knees too

effects.log: The bride takes the letter from your back, reads the silk prices, frowns, reads the knees, frowns harder, and reads the last line, and sits down under the willow. The silk prices, you think, were the point. They were the proof the line was true.

choices.text: Snake: speak it to the bride aloud instead, improved

effects.log: No prices. No knees. The snake turns it into something a poet would have been proud of, standing in the river with its head up in the dusk. The bride weeps. The tortoise says nothing at all, and the letter goes back across unopened.

choices.text: Both heads: deliver it as written, and the snake adds only the face it saw on the bank

effects.log: The letter, prices and knees and all. And then a black snake says, quietly, that the one who wrote it stood on the bank watching the river until there was nothing to watch. The bride laughs and cries at once, which is correct.

events.text: The bride ties a reply to your shell with a thread of red silk from her own sleeve. It is short. The snake reads it on the way back, of course. It says: the silk prices are too high, the merchant's mother should rub those knees with pine-resin oil, and I have been counting too, on the loom post, with chalk.

choices.text: Carry it back exactly

effects.log: The merchant reads it on the bank and laughs out loud, a big, foolish, happy laugh that carries all the way across the river and makes the bride, on the far bank, laugh too.

choices.text: Snake: carry it back, and say it improved

effects.log: The snake leaves out the prices and the pine-resin oil and puts in moonlight. The merchant is moved. The tortoise thinks the pine-resin oil was the best part.

events.text: The levy ends. The boats cross. On the far bank, under the big willow, {npc} and the bride bow to each other over a table with a bowl of clean water on it, the way weddings are done. The bride's grandmother, who is not sentimental, reads the letters aloud to the guests, all of them. If the snake improved anything, this is where the bride says, "But in the river you said..." and {npc} says, "What river?"

choices.text: Snake: own up, from the water, before the guests

effects.log: "I made it better," the snake says from the river, to a wedding. "The silk prices were better." The guests think it is a performance. The bride and the merchant know it is not, and laugh until they have to hold each other up.

choices.text: Say nothing. Let them have whatever they think they have

effects.log: They have a wedding and a story. The story has a talking river in it. Whether the river told the truth is the kind of thing a happy house can leave alone for years.

choices.text: Tortoise: look at the snake, until the snake looks away

effects.log: It takes a long time. The snake is stubborn. But in the end it looks away, at the willow, and the tortoise feels the coil round the shell tighten a little, which is how a snake blushes.

events.text: Forty years on, a grandchild of the house under the big willow comes down to the ford with a lacquered box of old letters, and sits on the landing stone, and reads them aloud to the river, one after another, because the family always said the river carried the first ones. Silk prices. Knees. Pine-resin oil. A wedding.

choices.text: Lie in the shallows and listen to all of it

effects.log: It takes all afternoon. You hear the whole of a household go by in letters, the quarrels and the harvests and the funerals, and at the end a short one: tell the turtle we were happy. The grandchild reads it to the turtle. It is the best letter you ever carried.

choices.text: Snake: ask the grandchild which version of the first letter the family keeps

effects.log: "Both," the grandchild says, surprised that a snake would ask. "Grandmother kept the real one in the box. Grandfather kept yours in his head. They argued about which was better for years." The snake is quietly delighted.

events.text: A sea turtle the size of a sedan chair comes up your river against the current, which no sea turtle does, wearing a black gauze official's hat tied under its chin with a ribbon. It bows three times, very slowly, on the gravel of your ford, and unrolls a scroll of kelp. "Byeolju, Registrar of the Water Palace, on behalf of His Majesty the Dragon King of the East Sea." It looks at your two heads, and then, carefully, bows once more, to the second.
events.arc: The Envoy in the Black Hat

choices.text: Both heads: bow back, one bow each

effects.log: "Two bows," says Byeolju, writing on the kelp with a claw. "Correct. Nobody ever does that." It is the beginning of a friendship that will last eleven hundred years and never once be called one.

choices.text: Snake: ask what the Dragon King pays

effects.log: Byeolju closes its eyes, as if the question gave it a mild headache. "Rank," it says. "Precedence. The use of the coral road. A hat." The snake wants the hat very badly and pretends not to.

choices.text: Tortoise: ask how long the post lasts

effects.log: "Until His Majesty says otherwise," says Byeolju, "and His Majesty has not said otherwise about anything for four hundred years." The tortoise finds this deeply reassuring.

events.text: The scroll says: the north water has had no envoy for an age. His Majesty wants one. The envoy carries the palace's word up every river north of the Han, to the river gods and the well gods and the dreams of magistrates; keeps the palace's manners; swears an oath at the coral gate. Byeolju adds, not from the scroll, that the last envoy of the north water was a catfish, and was eaten.
events.arc: The Envoy in the Black Hat

choices.text: Accept the post

effects.log: Byeolju writes your names on the kelp, both of them, in two columns, and rolls it up. "You will be sent for," it says. "Learn to hold your breath for a month." The tortoise already can.

choices.text: Accept, on condition you keep your own ford

effects.log: Byeolju considers this for a long time. "Irregular," it says. "Acceptable. Envoys must live somewhere." It writes a footnote on the kelp in very small characters.

choices.text: Not yet. The river needs you more than the sea does

effects.log: Byeolju bows, rolls up the kelp and starts the long swim home without a word of complaint. "Ten years," it says over its shoulder. "His Majesty will ask again. His Majesty asks everything again."

events.text: Ten years, almost to the day, and Byeolju comes up the river again in the same hat, with the same scroll, a little greyer around the edges of the shell. "His Majesty asks again," it says, "as foretold."
events.arc: The Envoy in the Black Hat

choices.text: Accept, this time

effects.log: "Excellent," says Byeolju, who had already written your names on the kelp before it left the sea. "Saves a third trip."

choices.text: Refuse again, politely

effects.log: Byeolju bows, and leaves you, as a parting gift, a single kelp leaf with the palace seal on it: a pass for the coral road, in case. You keep it under a stone for a hundred years.

events.text: Your first errand as envoy, with Byeolju beside you to see it done properly: the Dragon King's word to the god of a well in a village that has had no rain for two summers. The well god is a frog. The word is that rain is coming next month, and the well god must not let the villagers fill the well in. The villagers are already carrying baskets of stones.
events.arc: The Envoy in the Black Hat

choices.text: Tortoise: lie across the well-mouth until the rain comes

effects.log: A month on top of a well with a village throwing stones at you, which bounce. Then the rain comes. The villagers decide you were the rain's messenger, which is true, and build you a little shrine, which Byeolju considers irregular. (-6 health)

choices.text: Snake: tell the headman in a dream, the palace way

ok.log: The headman wakes up, puts down the stones, and orders the well dredged instead. Byeolju watches the snake do it and says, after a long silence, "You were born for this." The snake has to go and lie down.

fail.log: The headman dreams of a snake in a hat and wakes up screaming and fills the well faster. Byeolju has to go and sort it out in person, which takes three nights and a great many forms.

choices.text: Both heads: the snake speaks to the headman while the tortoise sits on the well, so they believe it

effects.log: A black turtle on the well-mouth and a voice from it telling them, very reasonably, to stop. The village stops. Byeolju writes in its report: "The north water's envoy works in pairs. Recommend this to other envoys." There are no other envoys with two heads.

events.text: Byeolju comes up the river one autumn with something wrapped in kelp and will not say what it is until the formalities are done: three bows, the scroll, the reading of the year's errands. Then it unwraps it. A black gauze official's hat, small, with a long ribbon to tie under a chin. "The envoy of the north water," says Byeolju, "will wear the hat of office. I had it made a little wide. I did not know which head."
events.arc: The Envoy in the Black Hat

choices.text: Tortoise: let Byeolju tie it on the tortoise's head

effects.log: Byeolju ties the ribbon with great care. The hat sits on the tortoise as if it had always been there. The snake looks at it out of the side of its eye for a hundred years.

choices.text: Snake: the snake wears it

effects.log: The hat on a snake's head is a sight the Water Palace never forgets. It slides off whenever the snake strikes, and the snake has to go back for it, with dignity, every time.

choices.text: Both heads: tie it on the shell, between the two

effects.log: Byeolju frowns at it for a long time and then writes a new regulation on the spot: the hat of office may be worn on the shell, by envoys with more than one head. It is the only rule in the Water Palace with a single subject.

events.text: Down the coral road, as Byeolju taught you: out past the river mouth, down the slope of the sea, a month of holding your breath in water so deep the light goes green, then blue, then nothing. Then a gate of red coral lit by pearls the size of melons, and two sea-bream guards with halberds who look at your two heads and then at each other.

choices.text: Tortoise: wait at the gate until you are announced

effects.log: It takes a day and a half to be announced, which Byeolju later tells you is very fast. The guards relax. An envoy who waits is an envoy who knows the place.

choices.text: Snake: talk your way past the guards before Byeolju arrives

effects.log: The snake tells the guards it is expected, which is true, and that it is in a hurry, which is not. They let you through. Byeolju finds you in the second courtyard and says nothing, very loudly.

events.text: The throne hall: pillars of nacre, a floor of mother-of-pearl, water so still you can hear the tide thinking. On the throne, a very old dragon who coughs. Along the walls, the court: a flatfish chancellor with both eyes on one side of its face, who therefore always looks at you sideways; an octopus who keeps the records with eight brushes at once; a family of mackerel who are all, apparently, ministers of something.

choices.text: Both heads: bow, one bow each, as Byeolju taught

effects.log: The old king laughs, a sound like a wave turning a stone. "Byeolju has taught them manners. Two bows. Somebody write that down." The octopus already has, eight times.

choices.text: Tortoise: bow slowly, so slowly the court gets nervous

effects.log: It is the longest bow in the history of the Water Palace. By the end of it the flatfish chancellor has decided you are either very wise or very slow, and is afraid to find out which.

choices.text: Snake: watch the court instead of the king, and learn who matters

effects.log: The king is old. The chancellor is ambitious. The octopus knows everything and says nothing. The mackerel are all related to the chancellor. Byeolju is the only honest official in the hall. The snake learns all this during one bow.

events.text: The oath of office is sworn at the coral gate, on the palace seal, in the hearing of the court. There is one oath for every envoy: to carry the Dragon King's word without adding or taking away. The tortoise wants to swear it as written. The snake wants to swear to serve the king's interest, which is a different thing, and a bigger one.

choices.text: Tortoise: swear it as written. Not one word added

effects.log: The snake says the words, because only the snake can, and says them exactly, and hates every one. It is the tortoise's oath in the snake's mouth. Byeolju nods once, satisfied.

choices.text: Snake: swear to the king's interest

effects.log: The flatfish chancellor smiles sideways. Byeolju does not. The tortoise feels the oath settle on the shell like a plate that is not quite straight.

choices.text: Both heads: one oath in two voices, the snake saying it and the tortoise meaning it

effects.log: The snake says the words and the tortoise holds them, and the court hears something it has never heard: one oath, sworn twice at once. The old king sits up on the throne for the first time in a year.

events.text: A banquet in the Water Palace: sea grapes, a soup the colour of moonlight, singing clams. The flatfish chancellor raises a cup and, sideways, a question: is it proper for the north water's envoy to be two officials drawing one salary? Or one official with two votes? The court goes quiet. The mackerel lean forward.

choices.text: Snake: answer, smoothly, that it is two officials drawing half a salary each

effects.log: The court laughs. The chancellor laughs too, a moment late. The snake is a success at court, from that night, in the way only very dangerous people are.

choices.text: Tortoise: say nothing, and go on eating sea grapes

effects.log: The silence goes on. The chancellor waits. You eat. In the end the old king says, "The envoy is eating," as if that settled something, and it does.

choices.text: Both heads: answer together, one sentence finished by the other

effects.log: "One shell," says the snake. "Two minds," says the tortoise, through the snake. "One salary," they finish, together. The court applauds. The chancellor never asks a question at dinner again.

events.text: The envoy of the north water has a room in the Water Palace: a small one, at the end of a long corridor of shells, with a window of clear crystal on the deep. Outside, the trench goes down and down into a black so complete that the pearls on the corridor walls stop at the window and will not look. Far down, something very large turns over in its sleep.

choices.text: Tortoise: lie at the window and watch the deep for a season

effects.log: Nothing happens, all season, in the most interesting way. The tortoise has never been so content. Something down there is older than the king, and patient, and the tortoise feels it notice you, once, and decide you are all right.

choices.text: Snake: ask Byeolju what sleeps down there

effects.log: "Nothing that is on any list," says Byeolju, which is the most frightening thing it has ever said. The snake does not ask again, and does not stop wondering for five hundred years.

events.text: The old Dragon King's cough becomes a fever. Fourteen physicians fail. The fifteenth, a catfish with whiskers to its fins, announces the only cure: the fresh liver of a land rabbit. The court turns, as one, to the only officials in the Water Palace who can walk on land. There are two. One is Byeolju. The other is you.

choices.text: Tortoise: say nothing, and let seniority decide

effects.log: Seniority decides, as it always does in the Water Palace. Byeolju is senior by three hundred years. A court painter paints a rabbit on silk so Byeolju will know one when it sees one. It has never seen a rabbit.

choices.text: Snake: volunteer at once. A trip to land, a rabbit, a liver!

effects.log: The tortoise, who does not want to go anywhere, is horrified. The court is impressed. Byeolju, who is senior, insists on going itself, out of duty and, you suspect, out of a wish to keep the snake away from anything with a liver.

choices.text: Both heads: offer to go together with Byeolju

effects.log: The chancellor rules that the north water's envoy is needed in the north water. Byeolju goes alone, with the painting rolled up in its shell. You walk it to the gate. It looks very small going up the coral road.

events.text: Byeolju comes back down the coral road with a rabbit on its shell: a white rabbit that was promised a ministry, a palace by the sea and a silk hat, and is wearing the hat. It takes one look at the throne hall, the coughing king, and the catfish sharpening a knife, and says: "Ah. My liver. Majesty, I would give it gladly. But as everyone knows, a rabbit takes out its liver each morning and washes it in a mountain stream, and mine is drying on a rock under a pine. If someone could take me back for it." The king believes every word. The snake is in love.

choices.text: Snake: say nothing. It is the best lie in a thousand years

effects.log: The snake catches the rabbit's eye across the hall. Something passes between them, one liar to one admirer of liars. The tortoise feels it pass and is a little jealous, which it did not know a tortoise could be.

choices.text: Tortoise: tell the king the truth: livers do not come out

effects.log: The king does not believe you. A rabbit in a hat is more convincing than a turtle in a hat. The snake hisses at the tortoise all the way home for spoiling it, and the rabbit is sent back for its liver anyway.

choices.text: Both heads: tell the king a better truth: a liver is only good fresh, so the rabbit must live

effects.log: The catfish cannot argue with that, and neither can the rabbit, who looks at you with sudden enormous respect. The rabbit is sent home alive, which it would have managed anyway, but now it owes you.

events.text: On the shore the rabbit leaps off Byeolju's back, throws the silk hat into the surf, and shouts from the top of a dune: "A liver outside the body! What fools live under the water!" Then it is gone into the pines. Byeolju sits on the wet sand. It cannot go home without a liver, and it cannot stay on land. You came up the coast after it, because the snake wanted to see this part.

choices.text: Tortoise: carry Byeolju home, and speak for it at court

effects.log: The snake speaks, and the tortoise decides every word: the rabbit was a master of strategy, no envoy could have caught it, and the fault is the catfish's for prescribing a liver that walks. Byeolju is not punished. It is given a medal, which it wears for a thousand years.

choices.text: Snake: go up into the pines after the rabbit, for a word with it

ok.log: You find it under a pine, very pleased with itself. "How," the snake asks. "Confidence," says the rabbit. "And a hat helps." The snake never forgets this. The tortoise wishes it would.

fail.log: The rabbit is long gone, and a fox is not. The snake has words with the fox instead, and comes back with a torn scale and no wisdom. (-4 health)

choices.text: Laugh, both heads, until the shore shakes

effects.log: Byeolju looks at you in outrage, and then, very slowly, its old mouth begins to twitch. By the time you reach the palace all three of you are still laughing, and the court thinks the envoys have gone mad from land air.

events.text: Fifty years later, in a market town on your river, a singer with a drum and a fan performs the whole story for a crowd on a straw mat: the sick king, the brave turtle official, the clever rabbit and its liver on a rock. It takes four hours. You are in it, for one line, as "a black turtle with two heads who held the inkstone and said nothing".

choices.text: Tortoise: lie under the bank and enjoy being the one who said nothing

effects.log: It is, the tortoise thinks, an excellent part. Nobody can say you played it badly.

choices.text: Snake: correct the singer, from the river, at the end

effects.log: "The snake said a great deal," says the river, as the crowd breaks up. The singer drops the fan. From then on, in that town, the turtle with two heads has a speech, and it is the funniest part of the song.

events.text: The kitchen men of a northern capital caught you at the river and dropped you down the prison well to keep its water sweet, as people do with turtles. The snake is beside itself. Above, the prison yard. Down the well, at night, comes a voice: {npc}, an envoy of a southern kingdom, held here because {he} came to ask the north for help against an enemy and would not give back a stretch of mountain land as the price. {He} talks to the well because there is nobody else.

choices.text: Tortoise: listen, every night, and say nothing

effects.log: The envoy talks about rivers in the south, about a queen who is clever and tired, about a friend who is a general and will come with an army if {he} is not home in sixty days. You listen. Wells are very good for listening.

choices.text: Snake: answer {him}, quietly, from the dark water

effects.log: "Sixty days," says the well. {npc} sits down very suddenly on the edge of the well-stone. Then, being a diplomat, {he} asks the well its name.

choices.text: Try to climb the well wall, to get out of this

effects.log: A turtle cannot climb a well. You learn this three times. The envoy hears the splashes and says, to the dark, "You too?" (-5 health)

events.text: {npc} has been in the cell above the well for forty days. The guards say the king of the north will have {him} executed if the land is not signed over, and {npc} will not sign. At night {he} lowers the well bucket, not for water, but to have something to hold on to.

choices.text: Tortoise: climb into the bucket and let {him} draw you up

mem.note: kept me company from the well
