effects.log: {npc} draws up the bucket and finds a black turtle in it, very heavy, with a snake wound round it, both heads looking at {him}. {He} laughs, for the first time in forty days, and lets you down again gently.

choices.text: Snake: tell {him} the guards' names, and which one takes gifts

effects.log: The snake has been listening to the guards for weeks. One of them likes cloth. One owes money. One has a brother in the palace. {npc} writes it all down on {his} sleeve with a burnt stick.

choices.text: Lie still at the bottom. Envoys come and go

effects.log: The bucket comes down every night and goes up empty. You feel the envoy's hope go up and down on the rope, and say nothing, and are not sure it was the right nothing.

events.text: A courtier of the north called Seon Dohae comes to the cell at night with food and rice liquor, paid for with a bolt of blue cloth {npc} smuggled in. They eat together. Then, as if idly, Seon Dohae tells a story: the Dragon King fell sick, the turtle went ashore for a rabbit's liver, the rabbit said it had left its liver on the mountain, and the turtle carried it back to fetch it. Then the courtier goes. {npc} sits in the dark, puzzled. {He} has not understood.

choices.text: Snake: whisper the rest of it up the well

effects.log: "The rabbit promised to come back with the liver," says the well, very softly. "It only had to get to the shore." There is a long silence above. Then {npc} begins, quietly, to laugh.

choices.text: Tortoise: let {him} find it alone. It is {his} escape

ok.log: It takes {npc} until dawn. Then you hear {him} say "Oh," very quietly, and then call for ink.

fail.log: Dawn comes and {npc} still does not see it, and the snake cannot bear it, and whispers it up the well anyway: the rabbit only had to reach the shore. The tortoise lets it. Some silences cost too much.

choices.text: Both heads: the tortoise taps the well-stone in the rhythm of the story while the snake says one word: "shore"

effects.log: One word, and a slow knocking like a turtle walking. {npc} sits up. "The shore," {he} says. "The rabbit only had to reach the shore." {He} calls for ink before the sun is up.

events.text: {npc} writes to the king of the north: the land is not mine to give, but let me go home and I will persuade my queen to give it back. The king believes {him}. On the morning {he} is freed, {npc} asks the guards to draw a bucket from the well to wash in before the road, and draws you up in it, and carries you out of the gate under {his} robe. At the border river, with the north's escort watching from the far bank, {he} sets you in the water.

choices.text: Tortoise: wait at the ford and watch {him} cross

effects.log: You watch {npc} cross the border river on a borrowed horse, and on the far bank turn and call to the escort that {he} will never give them the land, and ride south laughing. A road home. That night the plate over your left shoulder warms. (The Ox plate: a crossing, written true.)

choices.text: Snake: follow {him} as far as the next river, to see if {he} keeps the promise

effects.log: {He} does not keep it, of course. That was the point of the rabbit. The snake is delighted. The tortoise thinks of the king of the north, waiting for a liver.

choices.text: Both heads: see {him} across, and then speak once: "Remember the well"

effects.log: "I will remember the well," {npc} says from the far bank, "as long as I live, and longer." You do not know yet how much longer. (The Ox plate: a crossing, written true.)

events.text: Twelve years on, a word comes up the rivers, from fish to fish and ferry to ferry: in the south, the envoy who escaped the northern prison by the rabbit's trick has been made king. They say {he} keeps a black turtle carved in jade on {his} writing table, and will not say why.

choices.text: Tortoise: be glad, quietly, in the black sand

effects.log: A king who remembers a well. The tortoise is glad in the way stones are glad in the sun, without telling anyone.

choices.text: Snake: take some of the credit, to every fish who will listen

effects.log: By the time the story reaches the sea, the snake taught the king everything he knows. Byeolju hears it in the Water Palace and sends a very dry note.

events.text: The snake leads you overland one autumn, three nights from any river, and will not say why until you are there: a field of royal mounds, green and enormous, like a herd of sleeping hills. It is very quiet. The snake says this is Emptiness's own country, the mansion of tombs and weeping, and that a plate is not written by staying in your pool.

choices.text: Tortoise: lie among the mounds and feel how old they are

effects.log: Kings, queens, a prince who died at nine. The mounds do not mind you. They are the only things you have ever met that are better at waiting than the tortoise.

choices.text: Snake: go round every mound and taste the doors

effects.log: Most of the stone doors taste of earth and nothing. One, at the north end of the field, tastes of new lamp-oil and wet pigment. Someone is inside a tomb that is not finished.

events.text: A royal funeral comes into the field at dawn: banners, a bier on forty shoulders, hemp-clad mourners walking in the order of their grief, the wailers paid and the wailers not paid, and a little prince of five in a hemp hat too big for him, holding someone's hand. They lay a queen in the newest mound. It takes all day. Then the field is empty again.

choices.text: Watch it all, from the grass at the foot of the mound

effects.log: All day, every bow and every handful of earth, the little prince falling asleep on a mourner's shoulder before the end. You write none of it with a brush. The shell writes it. (The Emptiness plate: a funeral, written true.)

choices.text: Snake: write it quick and go, before the guards walk the field

effects.log: The snake writes it after the bier, before the end, from what a funeral usually is. It leaves out the little prince. It did not see him fall asleep. The plate cracks in the first frost. (The Emptiness plate, cracked.)

choices.text: Slip away. A queen's funeral is not for turtles

effects.log: You go back into the long grass. Behind you the wailing goes on until dark. It is a long way to any river from here, and you are glad of every step of it.

events.text: Night, and a lamp in the mouth of the unfinished tomb at the north end of the field. Inside, on a scaffold of poles, a painter is painting the walls of the burial chamber by the light of one oil lamp: an azure dragon on the east wall, a white tiger on the west, a red bird on the south. The north wall is bare plaster. The painter keeps looking at it and putting the brush down.

choices.text: Crawl in and watch from the doorway

effects.log: Mineral blue, iron red, white of lime. The painter works until the lamp gutters and never once looks at the doorway. You are very still. You are good at being very still.

choices.text: Snake: taste the pigment in the pots

effects.log: The blue tastes of copper and the red of rust, and the black, in a pot nobody has opened yet, tastes of pine soot and cold water and something like your own shell. The snake does not like that at all.

choices.text: Leave the painter in peace

effects.log: You go back into the grass. From the field you can see the lamp in the tomb mouth all night, a small warm square in all that dark. You think about the bare wall for a long time.

events.text: The painter sees you. A black turtle in the doorway of a tomb at midnight, a black snake wound round it, both heads turned to watch the work. The painter does not scream. The painter sits down very slowly on the scaffold, picks up a stick of charcoal, and begins to draw you on a board, fast, before you go.

choices.text: Tortoise: hold still for it, the whole night

effects.log: Board after board, by one lamp. At dawn the painter puts down the charcoal and bows to you, to the ground, and says, to the bare north wall: "So that is what goes there."

choices.text: Snake: turn the snake head round to face the tortoise, and see what the painter does

effects.log: The two heads, facing each other, for the first time in your life, because the snake wanted to see what it looked like on a board. The painter makes a sound like someone stepping on a thorn and draws until the charcoal is gone.

choices.text: Go, before the drawing is finished

effects.log: You back out of the tomb mouth into the grass. Behind you the charcoal keeps scratching. The painter has seen enough. You have a feeling you will meet that wall again.

events.text: Three men from a medicine shop in the county town wade your stretch of river with long-handled nets and a bamboo cage. Turtle shell, ground fine, is good for weak bones and night sweats, and an old one fetches a price. They are not diviners. They are worse: they do not care what the shell says.

choices.text: Tortoise: draw in under the bank roots and wait

effects.log: A net sweeps the roots twice. You are a stone among stones. By evening they have three small pond turtles and a bad temper, and they go home.

choices.text: Snake: strike at the first hand that comes near

effects.log: A black snake comes out of the water at a man's wrist. He drops the net and sits down in the river. The shop decides your stretch is not worth the wages.

choices.text: Get ahead of them and let the small pond turtles out of the cage

ok.log: The snake works the cage-peg loose while the men are arguing about lunch. Three pond turtles go back into the river. Nobody notices until the town.

fail.log: A net comes down over half of you. You tear out of it with the snake biting and the tortoise pulling, and lose a strip of skin from a hind leg. (-8 health)

events.text: A boy from the mill sits on the landing stone every evening with a line baited with a frog, because the medicine shop will pay a string of coins for a turtle as big as a winnowing tray, and his mother is sick. The frog is very fat. The snake has not eaten all day.

choices.text: Snake: take the frog off the hook, clean, every evening

effects.log: Every evening, a bare hook. The boy thinks the river is laughing at him. The river is.

choices.text: Tortoise: let him see you, and go under, and not come back up

effects.log: He sees a shell far too big to land on a frog line, and goes very pale, and winds in, and does not come back. A boy who knows his own size will live a long time.

choices.text: Leave a dead carp from the deep pool on the landing stone for him

effects.log: He finds the carp in the morning and stands looking at the river for a long while. His mother eats well for a week. He never fishes for turtles again, and never says why.

events.text: A cart comes along the river road with a brazier lashed to the back of it and four men with nets walking beside: a diviner's men, from a county yamen. Small diviners need shells too. They camp at the ford and ask the ferry about the old turtle, and the ferry, which has learned, says there is no such turtle.

choices.text: Tortoise: go down into the deep pool and sleep until they leave

effects.log: A month at the bottom of the pool in the cold. They drag the shallows, find nothing, and go on to the next river. The ferry family sends a bowl of rice down the bank in thanks for not being found.

choices.text: Snake: get into their camp at night and spill the brazier

ok.log: Hot coals on wet straw, a great deal of steam, four men dancing. In the morning the brazier is in the river and the men are on the road home, telling each other the ford is cursed.

fail.log: A dog in the camp. The snake gets away; the tortoise, attached, is slower, and takes a kick and a net-pole before you reach the water. (-10 health)

events.text: Someone has driven sharpened stakes into the sand round your sunning rock, points up and hidden under a skim of water, so that anything heavy that slides off the rock in a hurry lands on them. A hunter's trick for otters. The snake noticed the new sand. The tortoise did not.

choices.text: Snake: pull the stakes out one by one, at night

effects.log: Nine stakes, one a night, carried off to the deep pool. The hunter comes back, finds bare sand, and stands scratching his head. The tortoise thanks the snake, which it does not often do, and the snake pretends not to hear.

choices.text: Tortoise: find a new sunning rock

effects.log: There are other rocks. The new one is colder and has a better view of the ferry. The tortoise decides it always preferred it.

events.text: A water snake passing down the river in the spring flood stops on your rock to rest, and talks, the way travellers do. Upstream, three days, in a gorge, there is a pool, and in the pool a serpent who has waited five hundred years to become a dragon. An Imugi. It was a snake like any other once, the water snake says. Like you, it says to the snake, and does not even look at the tortoise.

choices.text: Snake: ask everything about the pool

effects.log: Where the gorge is. How deep the pool. How long a snake has to wait. The water snake answers everything and goes on downriver, and the snake lies on the rock the rest of the day and does not say one word to the tortoise.

choices.text: Tortoise: slide off the rock into the deep, and take the snake with you

effects.log: The snake has no choice. It never has. That is the whole trouble, and you both feel it, at the bottom of the pool, in the cold.

choices.text: Both heads: listen together, and then talk about it, together

effects.log: It is the hardest conversation you have ever had, and you have it under the ice all winter. It does not finish. But it is a conversation, and not a silence.

events.text: The snake goes quiet. Not silent, the snake is never silent, but quiet: it answers, it eats, it reads the eddies, and it does not tell the tortoise anything it does not have to. A whole year of that. At night it lies with its head on the shell and its eyes on the upstream bend, and the tortoise can feel it counting the days to a pool it has never seen.

choices.text: Tortoise: wait it out. Snakes get over things

effects.log: Snakes do not get over things. Snakes coil round them. By the end of the year the quiet has become a habit, and the tortoise realises it has waited out the wrong thing.

choices.text: Let the heads talk, all winter, about anything but the pool

effects.log: Stones on the riverbed, stories, the price of salt at the ferry. Never the pool. By spring the snake laughs at something the tortoise says, and you both pretend not to notice how long it has been.

choices.text: Snake: "Take me to see it. Only to see"

effects.log: The tortoise says yes before it can think about it, which is how you know it was the right answer, or at least the only one.

events.text: Three days upstream, in a gorge full of red leaves, the pool. Black water under a little waterfall. Something long lies along the bottom, longer than the pool should hold, and lifts a head the size of a door, and looks at your snake, and only at your snake. "Come," it says. "Uncoil. Be a dragon. You are already a serpent; you only have to let go of the stone."

choices.text: Snake: listen to it. Really listen

effects.log: The snake listens until dark. It does not uncoil. But it loosens, a little, the way a knot loosens before it comes undone, and the tortoise feels every turn of it.

choices.text: Tortoise: turn round and walk home, slowly, with the snake

effects.log: The tortoise turns before the snake can answer. The snake looks back at the pool all the way down the gorge. The serpent in the pool does not call after it. It has waited five hundred years. It can wait.

choices.text: Both heads: "We are already something. Something you have never seen"

effects.log: The serpent in the pool looks at you, at both of you, for a long time. "No," it says at last. "I have not." It sinks. On the way home the snake winds one turn tighter than it has ever been.

events.text: Years after, on a still night under the ice, the snake says, out of nothing: "I would have been alone in that pool for five hundred years." The tortoise waits. "And then a dragon. Alone in the sky." A long pause. "You snore," says the snake, "but you are there."

choices.text: Tortoise: say nothing, and be there

effects.log: It is the right nothing. It is warm, like a stone in the sun, in the middle of winter.

choices.text: Snake: finish it: "So I stayed"

effects.log: The snake says it out loud so it is said. Some things only become true when one of you says them and the other hears.

events.text: Downriver, at the next ford, the ferryman drowned in the spring flood, and the ferry passes to {npc}, eighteen, the drowned ferryman's daughter, because there is nobody else and because {he} says so to the headman in a voice that does not invite discussion. {He} rows, not pulls: a long scull oar at the stern, standing, the way the coast people do. The first week {he} goes round in a circle twice in front of the whole village.

choices.text: Tortoise: lie under the ferry and steady it, every crossing

effects.log: The second week {npc} goes straight across every time, and the village stops laughing. {He} thinks {he} has got the knack. {He} has, mostly. The rest is under the boat.

choices.text: Snake: watch how {he} handles the oar, and learn the current from it

effects.log: The snake learns more about the river by watching {npc} lose to it than by forty years of swimming in it. By autumn {npc} stops losing.

events.text: The flood comes up brown in the night, and at midnight someone hammers on the ferry house door: a midwife is needed on the far bank, now. {npc} looks at the river, which is a roaring field of brown, and takes the oar off the wall.

choices.text: Tortoise: get under the boat and hold it, whatever the river does

ok.log: The boat crosses a flood that should have taken it, straight as a plank, with something under it that the midwife feels through the hull and does not mention. A child is born on the far bank before dawn.

fail.log: A log in the flood hits you broadside under the boat. You hold on. The boat lands two hundred paces downstream, but it lands. (-14 health)

choices.text: Snake: go ahead of the boat and nose the floating logs aside

effects.log: All the way across, the logs that should have hit the boat turn aside a moment before. {npc} sees a black head in the flood once, pushing a branch away, and says nothing to the midwife.

events.text: {npc} is past forty now, broad-shouldered from the oar, with children who row badly. {He} knows there is something under the water. {He} has known for twenty years. Every evening {he} leaves a rice ball on the landing stone, and talks to the river while {he} ties up: the price of salt, a son who will not settle, a knee that aches before rain.

choices.text: Tortoise: eat the rice ball, every evening, and listen

mem.note: listened to me from the river

effects.log: Twenty years of evenings. {npc} never sees you, and never needs to. The rice ball is always gone. That is the whole of the conversation, and it is enough.

choices.text: Snake: answer {him}, once, about the knee

effects.log: "Pine-resin oil," says the river. {npc} drops the rope. Then {he} picks it up, ties it off, and says, "Thank you," as if it were the most ordinary thing, and the next evening there are two rice balls.

choices.text: Show yourself, once, sunning on the landing stone

effects.log: {npc} comes down in the morning and finds a black shell the size of a winnowing tray on the landing, with a snake round it. {He} stands still a long time. Then {he} sits down beside it and has breakfast.

events.text: {npc} is old. One autumn morning {he} rows the ferry over for the last time, with a grandchild at the oar beside {him}, learning. On the far bank {he} steps off, and puts the oar in the grandchild's hands, and does not get back in. {He} sits on the landing stone over there and watches the grandchild row back alone. Decades of the same crossing, ending.

choices.text: Hold the boat steady one last time, under the grandchild, and watch it all

effects.log: The grandchild goes in a circle twice. Then straight across. On the far bank {npc} laughs, the first time you have heard {him} laugh since {he} was eighteen. A crossing ends and a crossing begins. (The Ox plate: a crossing, written true.)

choices.text: Snake: cross to the far landing and sit with {him} while {he} watches

effects.log: An old ferry woman and a black snake on a landing stone, watching a child row. {npc} talks about the first week, the two circles. The snake says it remembers. {npc} says, "I know."

choices.text: Let the grandchild find the current alone

effects.log: You stay in the deep and let the boat go where the oar sends it. It goes round twice. It lands. Some crossings must be made without anything underneath.

events.text: The river is a border this year, with the war on the far side of it and watchtowers on both banks, and no boats allowed. On the near bank, {npc} weaves hemp under the eaves of a house by the water. {He} was promised to a herdsman from the far bank; the wedding was set for autumn; then the war. On the seventh night of the seventh month {npc} sets a bowl of clean water on a little table outside, and bows to the two stars that are parted by a river in the sky, and says to them that at least they get one night.

choices.text: Listen from the water, all night

effects.log: The stars do get one night. Magpies and crows make a bridge of themselves, the story says, and the Herdsman and the Weaver cross it, and it rains in the morning because they weep. {npc} tells the stars the whole story as if they did not know it.

choices.text: Snake: speak, from the water: "The river can carry one"

effects.log: {npc} knocks the bowl over. Then, very carefully, {he} rights it and fills it again and sits down facing the river. "When?" {he} says. The snake says: next year, on this night.

events.text: The seventh night of the seventh month, a year on. Rain in the afternoon, which the old women say is the Weaver star crying early. The magpies have flown off somewhere, as they do this time of year, to be a bridge. The watchtowers on both banks have lit their fires. {npc} has sent word across, by a fisherman who pretends to be deaf, that the herdsman is to come down to the far bank at the second watch and stand in the water.

choices.text: Tortoise: swim over at dusk and wait under the far bank

effects.log: Under the far bank, in the reeds, below a watchtower. At the second watch a young herdsman comes down to the water, shaking, and stands in it to the knees, and says, to the dark, "Hello?"

choices.text: Snake: go first and count the sentries on the far tower

effects.log: Four sentries, one asleep, one drinking, one homesick, and one who watches the water. The snake marks the one who watches the water, and counts the breaths between its turns.

events.text: The herdsman is on your back in the dark, holding the snake like a rope, wet to the waist and praying under his breath. Midriver, a torch moves on the far tower, and then another. Someone has heard something. An arrow goes into the water beside you with a sound like a fish jumping.

choices.text: Tortoise: go under, with him holding his breath, and walk the bottom

ok.log: He holds on and holds his breath, and you walk the black riverbed with him flat on your back. You come up under the near bank among the reeds. He is half-drowned and laughing.

fail.log: He lets go to breathe. The snake gets him by the collar; an arrow gets the edge of your shell, and then another. You land him on the near bank anyway. (-14 health)

choices.text: Snake: swim on the surface, fast, and trust the gap in the sentry's turns

effects.log: The snake counted the turns. The one who watches the water is looking downstream when you pass. The arrow was the drinker, shooting at a fish.

choices.text: Both heads: the tortoise swims low while the snake talks to the far tower, a frog's voice in the reeds

effects.log: The sentries hear a loud, rude frog and laugh and put the torches down. Midriver, the herdsman has to bite his own sleeve not to laugh too.

events.text: A wedding in the back room of a house by the river, with the shutters closed, because of the war. A table with a bowl of clean water, a pair of wooden ducks, a rooster wrapped in cloth that keeps trying to leave. {npc} in a red jacket borrowed from a neighbour, the herdsman in a borrowed hat. They bow to each other: two bows, then one, then the cup shared. Through a gap in the shutter, a black head watches from the river.

choices.text: Watch it all, to the last bow

effects.log: Every bow, the cup, the rooster escaping at the end and the whole wedding chasing it. That night the plate below your right shoulder warms and is written. (The Girl plate: a wedding made, written true.)

choices.text: Snake: leave early. Write it later from the sound of it

effects.log: The snake writes it from the laughter and the rooster. It gets the bows wrong. It cracks in the first frost. (The Girl plate, cracked.)

choices.text: Both heads: when they come out to bow to the river, bow back, both heads

effects.log: At the end they come out in the dark and bow to the river, and the river bows back, twice. {npc} weeps. The herdsman says rivers were always polite, everyone knows that. (The Girl plate, written true.)

events.text: A thousand corvee labourers from three counties come to your river with A-frames and straw baskets and build a dyke across the flood plain, so that the low fields below can be planted and a new village built there. They work from frost to frost, and sing the earth-tamping song, and an overseer on a horse rides up and down with a red flag. The snake watches the dyke grow for a year, tastes the water seeping at its foot, and says: it will fail. The third spring, at the sluice.

choices.text: Tortoise: "Then we will see it fail"

effects.log: The tortoise is already looking at the sluice, and where to lie, and how far from the breach. The snake wishes, for once, that the tortoise would argue.

choices.text: Snake: "Or we could make sure it fails now, before they build the village"

effects.log: It is a cold idea, and a kind one. A dyke that fails empty kills nobody. The tortoise does not say no. It does not say yes, either.

choices.text: Both heads: "Or we could make sure it holds"

effects.log: Neither head has ever stopped an ending before. Both of them want to see if it can be done.

events.text: The village goes up below the dyke: forty houses, a well, a shrine, children. The seep at the foot of the sluice is a trickle now, brown, and every night it is a little wider. The overseer rides past it every day and does not look down.

choices.text: Tortoise: push stones into the seep every night

effects.log: Stone after stone from the riverbed, carried in your mouth to the foot of the dyke. The seep slows. It does not stop. You know already that a turtle with stones is not enough. You do it anyway.

choices.text: Snake: tell the overseer, from the sluice, in the night

effects.log: The overseer hears a voice from the sluice telling him the dyke will fail. He has a man flogged for playing tricks, and posts a guard, and does nothing about the seep. The village hears about the voice, though. Some of them move their grain jars uphill.

choices.text: Snake: open the seep wider, now, while the fields are bare

effects.log: The tortoise refuses to help, and so the snake does it alone, as far as it can reach. The seep runs brown all winter. The overseer still does not look down.

choices.text: Watch, and wait for the third spring

effects.log: You lie in the river below the sluice and watch the seep. It is very small. It is going to be very large.

events.text: The third spring. Snowmelt and rain together, the river higher than anyone has seen it, and at midnight the sluice of the dyke gives way with a sound like a cart full of stones going over a cliff. The water goes through the gap toward the forty houses.

choices.text: Watch it go: the gap, the water, the lanterns running uphill

effects.log: You see all of it, from the river under the breach: the earth going, the water finding the low fields, the lanterns of the village going up the hill in a long line. Most of them get up the hill. That night the plate low on your shell is written. (The Encampment plate: a great earthwork ending, written true.)

choices.text: Tortoise: lie in the breach with your shell against the water

ok.log: You go into the gap sideways and the water hits your shell and stops, mostly, for long enough. The village gets up the hill with its children and its grain and its shrine bell. Then you let go, and the dyke goes, and nobody is under it. No plate. A village.

fail.log: The water takes you through the breach like a leaf. You see all of it on the way, from inside the flood. You come to rest in a field a mile below with the plate on your back written and your shell scraped raw. (-20 health) (The Encampment plate, written true.)

choices.text: Snake: take you upriver on a hunch about frogs, and write it later from the river

effects.log: The snake took you upriver the week before, on a hunch about frogs. It writes the breach from what the river carries down: thatch, a cradle, a shrine bell. It cracks in the first frost. (The Encampment plate, cracked.)

events.text: They rebuild the dyke, three counties again, a new overseer. The new overseer walks the foot of it every evening and looks down. One evening the overseer finds a line of river stones laid along the foot of the sluice, each the size of a turtle's head, very neatly, and stands looking at them a long time, and then orders the whole foot of the dyke faced with stone in just that way.

choices.text: Tortoise: keep laying stones, every night, until they finish

effects.log: For a season you and three counties lay stones side by side, without either knowing about the other. The new dyke holds for three hundred years.

choices.text: Snake: watch the new overseer, and decide whether to trust anyone with a flag

effects.log: The new overseer gets off the horse. That, the snake decides, is the whole difference.

events.text: A boy of nine comes down to the ford to fill a water jar, and leans over to drink, and the snake, idly, reads {his} face in the river the way it reads eddies. Then it is not idle. Nineteen, it says. The year {he} turns nineteen. Not a sickness, not a river, not a blade: only the end of the number written next to {his} name. {npc} is the only child of the house with the persimmon tree.
events.arc: The Two Old Men at Baduk

choices.text: Tortoise: "Nineteen. Then we will be there"

effects.log: Ten years. The tortoise settles into the black sand under the ford to wait, as it always does. The snake watches the boy carry the water jar home up the bank, slopping it, and does not settle at all.

choices.text: Snake: read it again. Whose number? Written where?

ok.log: Written in a register, the snake says, slowly, as it comes. In a book kept by someone. Somewhere high. Numbers in a book can be changed. The snake has never been so interested in anything in its life.

fail.log: The face is gone from the water before the snake can look again. Nineteen is all it has. It is enough to ruin a whole autumn.

events.text: A wandering monk crosses at the ford with a staff and a gourd, and at the landing looks once at the face of the boy from the house with the persimmon tree, {npc}, grown tall now, and stops, and goes to the house. You hear it through the river: the parents weeping, the monk's low voice. Go up the mountain behind the village on the third day of the third month, the monk says, with a jar of good rice liquor and a plate of dried meat. Two old men will be playing baduk on the flat rock at the top. Serve them. Say nothing. Only when they have eaten, bow, and ask.
events.arc: The Two Old Men at Baduk

choices.text: Tortoise: follow the mountain stream up, on the day

effects.log: There is a stream from the top of that mountain to your ford. You will walk up the bed of it. It will take you a season. You start now.

choices.text: Snake: go up first, alone, and see who these old men are

effects.log: The snake stretches up the stream as far as it can from the shell and further, and comes back near dawn very quiet. It found the rock. There was nobody there. There was a board, with the stones still on it, warm.

choices.text: Stay at the ford. Some doors are not for turtles

effects.log: You watch {npc} go up the mountain path with the jar and the plate, on the day, alone. The snake does not speak to you until {npc} comes back down.

events.text: The flat rock at the top of the mountain, in a mist. Two old men in white robes playing baduk, so absorbed that they do not look up when {npc} kneels beside them with the jar. {npc} pours. They drink. {npc} sets down the dried meat. They eat. Neither of them looks at {him} once. You lie in the cold little pool at the head of the stream, where the water begins, and watch. One of them is fair-faced and smiles at the board. One of them is stern and ugly and frowns at it.
events.arc: The Two Old Men at Baduk

choices.text: Tortoise: watch the stern one

effects.log: The stern one sits very still, the way only something old and heavy sits, and moves a stone only when it is sure. The tortoise watches it for an hour and has the strangest feeling of looking down at its own feet.

choices.text: Snake: watch the fair one

effects.log: The fair one sits with one leg curled under the other, and the other under that, a coil of a sitter, and laughs when it takes a stone. The snake watches it and goes cold all down its length.

events.text: The game ends. The old men look up and see {npc}, and the empty jar, and the empty plate, and the stern one says: "We have eaten what was not ours." {npc} bows to the ground and asks. The fair one wants to help. The stern one refuses: a number is a number. They quarrel. They make it up, the way old friends do, by both pretending they had agreed all along. The stern one takes a book from a sleeve, a register of names, and the fair one takes the brush, and in front of {npc} and the mist and you, nineteen becomes ninety-nine.
events.arc: The Two Old Men at Baduk

choices.text: Tortoise: watch the brush, every stroke of it

effects.log: Two strokes. A one become a nine. That night the plate at the top of your shell, the first plate, the Dipper's, is written, and the characters on it are the same shape as the ones in the register. (The Dipper plate: a lifespan rewritten, written true.)

choices.text: Snake: read the register over their shoulders

effects.log: Names, and numbers, and on the page before the boy's, in the margin, two small marks the snake knows: a shell, and a coil. When it looks up, the stern one is looking straight at it, and the fair one is smiling. (The Dipper plate, written true.)

choices.text: Both heads: when the stern one looks up at the pool, bow, both heads, as to elders

effects.log: The stern one sees two heads bow from a pool at the head of a stream, and nods, slowly, the way the tortoise nods. The fair one laughs and says, "There. You see? They will do." You do not understand it for a thousand years. (The Dipper plate, written true.)

events.text: {npc} lives. Nineteen comes and goes like any other year. {npc} grows a beard, keeps the persimmon tree, has children, then grandchildren, and every spring on the third day of the third month climbs the mountain with a jar and a plate and sets them on the flat rock, and finds it empty, and comes down past the ford, and bows to the river on the way, for no reason {he} can give.
events.arc: The Two Old Men at Baduk

choices.text: Tortoise: bow back, every spring, from the black sand

effects.log: Decades of springs, bowing. {npc} is very old, at the end, and has to be helped up the mountain by grandchildren, and still bows to the river on the way down.

choices.text: Snake: say, one spring, "They were glad of the liquor"

effects.log: {npc}, old by then, stands very still on the bank. "I always thought," {he} says, "there was someone else on the mountain that day." The snake says nothing more, which for the snake is a kind of bow.

events.text: Late autumn, a raw grey evening, and the tortoise, half asleep in the shallows, thinks: I wish the ice would come. It is a thought it has had every autumn of its long life. In the morning the ford is frozen from bank to bank, a full day before it ever freezes, and the ice is thickest in a ring round your shell.

choices.text: Tortoise: lie very still, and feel it

effects.log: The cold is not outside you. It is a little bit yours, the way the shell is. You do not tell the snake. The snake knows anyway.

choices.text: Snake: "Do it again. On purpose"

effects.log: The tortoise tries, and the river does nothing at all for a week, out of what seems like spite. Then, when nobody is trying, it freezes again overnight. Winter, it turns out, listens. It does not obey.

events.text: The ferry family has noticed. The ice comes to your ford a day before it comes anywhere else on the river, every year now, and leaves a day later, and the ferry hand makes good money all winter carrying people across the ice on a sledge. The snake has noticed that the ferry hand has noticed, and has ideas.

choices.text: Snake: hold the ice a week late, for the ferry hand, for a share of the fish

effects.log: A week of extra ice. The ferry hand gets rich, by ferry standards, and leaves a basket of fish on the landing every month. The tortoise eats none of it, on principle, and then some of it, because it is very good fish.

choices.text: Tortoise: leave it be. The river is not a tool

effects.log: The ice comes and goes when it likes, mostly. The tortoise will not ask for more. The cold, as if it knew, comes a little closer anyway.

events.text: A hard year. The village upriver needs the ice to come early, to get their grain to the market town across the river before the price falls. The village downriver needs it late, to get their boats home from the coast. Both send their headmen to the ford with a bowl of rice and a request, because both have heard the same rumour.

choices.text: Tortoise: freeze it early. The grain cannot wait; boats can

effects.log: The ice comes early. The grain crosses. The downriver boats come home overland, cursing, a week late. The snake asks who pays. Nobody answers. It is the first time the snake asks that. It will not be the last.

choices.text: Snake: hold it late. The boats have men in them

effects.log: The boats come home. The grain goes to market late and cheap. The upriver headman leaves a bowl of rice at the ford anyway, which the snake finds harder to bear than a curse.

choices.text: Both heads: freeze only the upper ford, and leave the channel open for the boats

ok.log: A bridge of ice across the upper ford and a black open lane down the middle of the river below. Both villages get what they need. Neither ever knows the other asked.

fail.log: The ice will not divide itself. It comes everywhere, a day late for the grain and a day early for the boats. Everybody is a little worse off. Winter, it turns out, does not do halves. (-6 health)

events.text: The snake was right to the year. In the house by the ford an old ferryman of ninety, who has pulled the rope for seventy of them, lies down after supper and does not mean to get up. You are under his window in the reeds, where you have waited. His grandson is asleep in the next room.

choices.text: Tortoise: watch. See all of it. That is what you came for

effects.log: You do not look away once. When it is over, the plate is warm on your back, and then cold, and then written. What you saw, and nothing you did not.

choices.text: Snake: slip into the house and wake the grandson, so the herb doctor comes in time

effects.log: The grandson wakes to a black snake on his chest and runs for the herb doctor in his bare feet. The old man lives three more springs, and pulls the rope for all of them. No plate. The tortoise wanted the plate. It ate a rice cake instead.

choices.text: Both heads: the snake changes it, and the tortoise stays to see the new ending too

effects.log: The snake wakes the grandson, and the herb doctor comes in time. The tortoise stays in the reeds to watch what comes after: three more springs of the old man at the rope, an ending nobody read. No plate, and the tortoise finds that was worth giving up.

events.text: The plank bridge at the gorge, as the snake said: the spring flood coming down brown and full of trees, and the bridge shuddering on its old piles, and a pedlar with a pack starting across it, because he has always crossed there.

choices.text: Tortoise: watch. See all of it. That is what you came for

effects.log: You do not look away once. When it is over, the plate is warm on your back, and then cold, and then written. What you saw, and nothing you did not.

choices.text: Tortoise: get under the middle pile and hold it till the pedlar is over

effects.log: You hold the pile with your back against the flood until the pedlar is across. Then you let go, and the old bridge stays up, just. The county builds a stone one beside it that summer. No crossing ended. No plate.

choices.text: Both heads: the snake changes it, and the tortoise stays to see the new ending too

effects.log: The snake calls the pedlar back from the planks in a voice out of the reeds. He stands on the near bank, swearing, and watches the old bridge go into the flood with nobody on it. The tortoise watches too. No plate, and the tortoise finds that was worth giving up.

events.text: A wedding on the far bank, as the snake said, and a strange one. The weaver and the herdsman have been parted nine years by this river and the war on it. The bride's house is ready, the table set, the bowl of water poured; but the groom's party is stuck on the near bank at the ford because the ferry rope broke in the night. The snake read it: at sunset, rather than wait another year, they will be married across the water, each on a bank, bowing over the river.
